items.title: Recovering Edward Said’s Voice
items.summary:
For decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Said, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Now, as Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues, Said’s legacy is not just urgent, but also, in some spaces, the target of censorship . Today, author Moustafa Bayoumi, who studied under the late critic, activist, and professor at Columbia University, pens a thoughtful review of Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), a new documentary by Maiken Baird whose audio consists almost entirely of Said’s own words. “To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation,” Bayoumi writes.

Can contemporary art make us laugh (and not just when we’re making fun of it)? Greta Rainbow visits a New York exhibition that’s all about embracing humor in art, and somewhere between Brian Belott's absurdist fan-embedded assemblages and Ebecho Muslimova’s delightfully transgressive depictions, she learns a thing or two about her own funny bone.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

items.title: How Well Do You Know Your Artistic Icons?
items.summary:
With a world in crisis and an art market spinning out of control, ace art-world consultants Chen & Lampert deliver a quiz full of hard choices for Art in America readers from far and wide. 

The fall issue of Art in America honors artistic icons, and in recognition of their trailblazing singularity we’ve rejiggered the format of our usual quiz. Rather than answer questions about yourself, let’s find out what you know about the superstars, trendsetters, and groundbreakers whose audacity and cultural capital have reshaped the art world from a niche marketplace into a global duty-free mall. Correct answers are worth one point each, so tally up your score to find out how you fared.

1. He’s number one in our hearts for making number two in a metal can, sealing it shut, and calling it art: 

a) Piero Manzoni
b) Marcel Duchamp
c) Andy Warhol

2. This artist invented his own color and threatened to sue people for using it: 

a) Yves Klein
b) Anish Kapoor
c) Bob Ross

3. He locked himself inside a cage for a year as an artwork: 

a) Joseph Beuys
b) Tehching Hsieh
c) Henry Darger

4. This person’s art involved voluntarily picking up NYC garbage and cleaning the streets for fun: 

a) Pope.L
b) Mierle Laderman Ukeles
c) Yuji Agematsu

5. Interior Scroll is a performance classic in which this artist recites a rant retrieved from her vagina: 

a) Carolee Schneemann
b) Valie Export
c) Florentina Holzinger

6. This storied gallerist served prison time for tax evasion: 

a) Ileana Sonnabend
b) Mary Boone
c) Barbara Gladstone

7. Which prolific artist sired seven children with two wives…
items.t: How Well Do You Know Your Artistic Icons?

items.title: Is Donald Trump beyond caricature? Not at all – here’s his hilarious origin story
items.summary:
Ustinov Studio, Bath
Elliot Cowan is scarily convincing as the budding Potus in Donald, a high-speed, three-actor comedy from the playwright behind The Lehman Trilogy

His manner and actions often seeming like improbable caricature, the current US president sets a challenge for satire, any comic exaggeration likely to be trumped by reality. Mike Bartlett’s play The 47th (2022), staged between Trump’s administrations, pursued wild fantasies about the politician’s future career that were soon superseded by odder events. Ali Abbasi’s movie The Apprentice (2024) more sensibly focused on the period from 1973 to 1986 in which the New York realtor developed the behavioural and verbal tics that make him probably the most ridiculed figure in modern history, though such mockery, until the recent midterms, largely consoled detractors while being ignored by supporters.

Closer to Abbasi’s approach, Donald by the Italian dramatist Stefano Massini resembles his play The Lehman Trilogy – an international hit about the banking dynasty – in being a psychological analysis played by three actors with lightning switches of character and costume. In this case, the cut-up structure reflects…

items.title: Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.
items.summary:
It was an evening of superlatives at Sotheby’s, whose two auctions of Impressionist and modern art in New York tonight brought in a total of $777.8 million. 

That total is the highest one for a single night at the auction house, edging past the $706 million achieved last November at the house’s inaugural evening double-header at the Breuer building. And while the 12 lots from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection came in at $412 million, just shy of their presale low estimate of $414.5 million, those dozen works still managed to set a record for a single-owner evening sale dedicated to Impressionist and modern art at Sotheby’s. (Unless otherwise noted, prices cited here are inclusive of fees.)

Two lots in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection were the most anticipated paintings of the season: Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) and Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888–90). 

They both achieved eye-popping prices—$190.4 million for the van Gogh, the artist’s highest price to date and the highest price for any work of art ever sold at Sotheby’s, and $111 million for the Cézanne, the second-highest price for Cézanne at auction. But the bidding was anticlimactic. 

Both works hammered below their pre-sale estimates. There was just a smattering of bids on the van Gogh. The Cézanne inched along with four bids alternating between Sotheby’s specialists Lisa Dennison, Chairman Americas, and Helena Newman, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe. It hammered to Newman.

Asked after the sale whether the publicity surrounding the restitution claim against the van Gogh had affected bidding, Sotheby’s…
items.t: Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.

items.title: ‘We can rage’: Michael Sheen fires up the gripping medieval epic Owain & Henry
items.summary:
Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff
Sheen is in wondrous voice as Owain Glyndŵr, clashing with Henry IV, in Gary Owen’s stirring history play for Welsh National Theatre

No one does rousing like Michael Sheen. Whether urging on the Welsh World Cup squad or vowing “apocalypse” on The Traitors, he surges forward on waves of rhetoric. As Owain Glyndŵr, beacon of Welsh resistance, he doesn’t disappoint. “We can die gently and be forgotten,” he exhorts his followers. “Or we can rage.”

Rage and resignation, the sword and the song, resonate through Gary Owen’s absorbing medieval epic for Wales Millennium Centre and Sheen’s new Welsh National Theatre. Glyndŵr is a marginal figure in Shakespeare’s Henry IV plays, a thorn in the unstable king’s side. Here he stands central, a fitting protagonist for a moment of both surging populist politics and a disillusionment with power play.

items.title: A Tiny Monet With a Wild Backstory Just Fetched More Than 20 Times its Estimate at a Christie’s Day Sale
items.summary:
The auction houses’ marquee evening sales get all the headlines, with high-eight-figure artworks and high-nine-figure totals, sometimes approaching the billion-dollar mark when the market is flush.

But the more modest daytime sales of lower-priced materials occasionally contain real treasures. When I wrote about them for Artnet News in 2015, experts told me that this is where the houses make a lot of their profits; dealers haunt these sales to stock up on inventory; they are far less stage-managed than the evening events; they may be more indicative of the actual health of the market; and you can find better deals.

And they can occasionally spark serious bidding wars. On Wednesday, a tiny artwork by a titan of French Impressionism became the latest example.

Claude Monet’s La Barque (ca. 1874), which came under the hammer at Christie’s Rockefeller Center saleroom at a day sale of Impressionist and modern art, was estimated at $300,000 to $500,000, but fetched just shy of $7 million. Its modest estimate matched its diminutive size: it measures only 2¾ by 3½ inches, so it sold for $722,285.71 per square inch. 

More than 20 bidders fought for the tiny panel, some in the room and some bidding on the phone via Christie’s specialists, says the house; the contest went on for six minutes and 45 seconds, and Rachel White Young, head of the 20th-century evening sale, won the prize for her client.

Claude Monet, La Barque (ca. 1874). 

Even before making a little auction history on Wednesday, the painting had an unusual backstory.

Paris art dealer Georges Petit, a collector and…
items.t: A Tiny Monet With a Wild Backstory Just Fetched More Than 20 Times its Estimate at a Christie’s Day Sale

items.title: Cézanne ‘Arlequin’ Sells for $111 M. at Sotheby’s, Becoming One of the Most Expensive Paintings by the Artist
items.summary:
Paul Cézanne made his name painting apples and mountains. But on Wednesday night, the artist’s somewhat severe picture of a teenager in costume became one of the most expensive Cézannes ever sold at auction, after selling at Sotheby’s New York for $111 million with fees.

Arlequin (1888–90), a colorful painting of a young man in a red-and-black diamond-patterned costume, hit the block at Sotheby’s during its dedicated evening sale for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection. The painting hammered at $99 million.

It failed to beat the previous record of $137.8 million set by La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888–90), which sold at Christie’s in 2022 as part of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen’s collection. Still, once auctioneer Oliver Barker sold Arlequin tonight, a round of applause followed.

Sotheby’s didn’t publish an estimate for Arlequin prior to the sale, though the painting was expected to bring in around $120 million.

The figure in the painting is Cézanne’s son, Paul, dressed as Harlequin, the mischievous character from Italian commedia dell’arte theater. He wears a pointed hat and an elaborate white collar, and holds a slender baton as he walks across a sharply tilted floor. For someone dressed as a comic character, he looks surprisingly serious.

Cézanne painted the picture in Paris between 1888 and 1890, when he was experimenting with a series of theatrical subjects. There are only four paintings in the group, and Arlequin is the only one still in private hands. The others are in museums, including the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., the Pola Museum of Art in…
items.t: Cézanne ‘Arlequin’ Sells for $111 M. at Sotheby’s, Becoming One of the Most Expensive Paintings by the Artist

items.title: Van Gogh Slashes Auction Record at Sotheby’s, Selling for $190.4 M.
items.summary:
After a week dominated by a Nazi-era restitution dispute, Sotheby’s finally got to sell a $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting on Wednesday night—for more than it bargained for.

Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), a picture of chestnut trees in bloom painted just weeks before the artist’s death, sold for $190.4 million (including fees), setting a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The painting, which carried an undisclosed guarantee, hammered at $165 million against an expectation of around $180 million (pre-sale estimates do not include buyer’s fees).

After the sale, Kelly Crow reported in the Wall Street Journal that dealer William Acquavella was the painting’s buyer, something that ARTnews also independently confirmed.

The fifth item and cover lot for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” hung behind the rostrum presided over by auctioneer Oliver Barker.

The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Verger avec cyprès (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen , sold, hammering for $102 million.

Wednesday’s result beats that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

The record is certainly a victory for Sotheby’s, which almost wasn’t going to be able to sell Châtaigniers en fleurs . Last Thursday, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale , arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi…
items.t: Van Gogh Slashes Auction Record at Sotheby’s, Selling for $190.4 M.

items.title: Is My Art Funny to You?
items.summary:
Ebecho Muslimova, “Fatebe Blow and Float” (2024) (image courtesy the artist and Magenta Plains, New York) Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art , a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown , artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take…
items.t: Is My Art Funny to You?

items.title: Phillips Evening Sale Tops $104 M., Led By $44.6 M. Modigliani Sculpture
items.summary:
Phillips’s modern and contemporary evening sale, held at its Park Avenue headquarters in New York on Tuesday night, garnered $104.4 million with fees on 22 lots, led by a $44.6 million total for the 1911–12 Amedeo Modigliani sculpture Tête .

With one lot withdrawn prior to sale and only one lot going unsold, the sale posted a healthy 95 percent sell-through rate by lot and an even more impressive 99 percent sell-through rate by value.

In a post-sale email, the auction house, which has recently faced scrutiny following cost-cutting and a major leadership shake-up in August, touted the total as a 55 percent increase over the equivalent sale last year. That figure is correct, but it does not tell the whole story. The 2025 edition of the modern and contemporary evening sale generated $67.3 million on 33 lots with two unsold. This year’s edition was pulled up considerably by the Modigliani result. Remove that from the total and the take drops to $59.8 million, though that is spread across 20 lots rather than 31. Still impressive, all things considered, but not quite the mega-result the house is touting.

But credit where credit is due: Phillips specialists did secure that Modigliani consignment, and it significantly outperformed its $28–$35 million estimate. Other strong results for the night were the eight-panel David Hockney group portrait David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982 , which landed within its $10–$15 million presale estimate for a total of $12.2 million with fees; the Alexander Calder sculpture Snow Flurry, May 14 (1959), which reached $7.5 million with fees…
items.t: Phillips Evening Sale Tops $104 M., Led By $44.6 M. Modigliani Sculpture

items.title: A Marquee Week of Indulgence
items.summary:
My mom called me greedy in jest this weekend because I had the gall to eat … more than five (but fewer than 10!) square slices of a delicious ube cake in her presence. Unlike each savored bite of that addictive purple pastry, I took her criticism on the chin because I believe that greed and indulgence function as a Venn diagram rather than as synonyms. And because there was still plenty of cake to go around.

Indulgence is in the air right now, and not just because we’re closing in on Thanksgiving weekend. Marquee auctions have rolled in like a thick fog on Monday, not long after the ADAA fair and an adjunctive torrential downpour rinsed the last of art fair season out of New York late last week. A press release from Sotheby’s informed me that $1.1 billion worth of art will go under the hammer this month, underpinned by today’s sale of a rarely seen van Gogh landscape expected to fetch a record-breaking $180 million. A brief shakeup ensued less than a week before the painting goes to auction, as the descendants of its former owner suddenly called on Sotheby’s to withdraw the work , alleging that it was sold under duress due to Nazi persecution. 

Don’t worry, though — the auction house shared in a follow-up release that the descendants and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, who are selling the painting alongside 11 other multimillion-dollar masterpieces from their collection, have come to a “mutually satisfactory resolution” that allows the sale to proceed as scheduled.

Really glad they worked that out. 

On the other side of the same coin, protesters gathered outside of the…
items.t: A Marquee Week of Indulgence

items.title: Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Never Stopped Innovating, Dies at 89
items.summary:
In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world. 

Arpita Singh (1937–2026)
 Indian painter who bridged fantasy and reality 

One of the most high-profile contemporary Indian artists, Singh fused violent realism and fantasy imagery, constantly innovating across a six-decade career. In the 1970s and '80s, for instance, she explored abstraction, producing spare compositions filled with dots and dashes. She became more widely known in the West due to an exhibition at Serpentine Galleries just last year. 

"Singh never settles into a mode or style," critic John Yau wrote in a 2017 review of her exhibition at New Delhi- and New York-based Talwar Gallery for this magazine. "This body of work, which is being shown for the first time in America, is a singular achievement."
items.t: Arpita Singh, Indian Painter Who Never Stopped Innovating, Dies at 89

items.title: MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years
items.summary:
The indelible impact of late Cuban-American artist Ana Mendieta 's practice will be celebrated in a forthcoming retrospective in New York next year. Scheduled to open at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in Manhattan in December 2027, Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective marks the first presentation of Mendieta's overarching career in the United States in over 20 years. 

MoMA's announcement comes just two months before Tate Modern's ongoing Mendieta retrospective closes in London. Comprising around 200 works, including rarely seen formative drawings and newly remastered films, the MoMA exhibition will present Mendieta's artistic process, signature developments, and career milestones in a chronological fashion. Starting with early figurative works completed during her undergraduate and graduate studies at the University of Iowa, the exhibition will follow the artist's subsequent expansion in making and documenting her performance art, as well as her foray into sculpture, installation, and site-specific land art.

Born in Cuba and raised in Iowa from age 12 as a child evacuee through Operation Peter Pan, Mendieta ruminated on themes of displacement, ancestral memory, ecology, and the politics of the female body, as well as its connection with the natural world. She's best known for her Silueta (1973–80) series, in which the outline of her body (either present or absent) is embedded, extruded, burned, or embellished into various natural environments as a physical and spiritual reunion with the earth. These “earth-body works,” as Mendieta called them, dealt with Mesoamerican and…
items.t: MoMA to Host First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Over 20 Years

items.title: Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever
items.summary:
In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument , filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die.  

While Salloum and Suleiman’s film consists mostly of news clips and film reels, one of Gaza’s elder statesmen, the late Haider Abdul Shafi, does appear briefly twice. In one scene, Abdul Shafi, sitting at a nondescript table, is asked by an interviewer: “Is it your belief that if a Palestinian state was created, there would be lasting peace in the Middle East?” Just as he’s about to respond, the film mischievously cuts away, in an edit loaded with meaning. Palestinians may be seen in Western media, the film is telling us, but they cannot be heard from.

Maiken Baird’s new documentary, Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), joyfully demonstrates how Edward Said was the exception to this semi-official ban on Palestinians representing themselves. Like Salloum and Suleiman, Baird also sifts through reservoirs of found footage, though the result couldn’t be more different. Offering a rough chronology of Said’s life, Baird’s film celebrates him by highlighting his contributions and lasting influence in numerous domains, from literary theory to American foreign policy. 

For decades, the Columbia University professor of comparative literature was the most famous, if not the only, Palestinian…
items.t: Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

items.title: Nina Kintsurashvili's Paintings of Yearning
items.summary:
Copious research materials drawn from her country’s rich and complex history are integral to Georgian painter Nina Kintsurashvili. She doesn’t depict them — including ancient frescoes, Byzantine icons, earthenware vessels, books, or Soviet-era illustrations — but instead obliquely alludes to, channels, and transforms them in largely abstract yet partially figural paintings. 

Her new paintings (all oil on linen from 2026) are luscious yet willfully scruffy, with paint often applied thickly and sometimes erased, and with brushstrokes ranging from vigorous and broad to wispy and spindly. In “Rifts,” creamy, sinewy, irregularly shaped forms spread horizontally from border to border. Underneath, multicolored vertical bands pull the picture plane downward, as if under gravity. There is motion here — pressure, tension — a shifting terrain. At the very bottom is something curious, which crops up often in these works: a grid, or rather a snippet of a grid. It could be the magnified warp and weft of the linen. It could be a section of fence. 

Installation view of Nina Kintsurashvili: Seams at Chapter NY
items.t: Nina Kintsurashvili's Paintings of Yearning

items.title: Trump Accepts Artistic Gift from India Just Months After Branding it a “Hellhole” Country
items.summary:
Traditional Indian art and crafts were in the spotlight as Indian prime minister Narendra Modi arrived at the ASEAN Summit and meeting of Quad leaders, which concluded yesterday in Manila, the capital of the Philippines. It was organized by Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which includes 11 countries in the region, whose populations total almost 700 million.

Modi gave out gifts to all the leaders in attendance. Philippines president Ferdinand R. “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. got a hand-knotted Kashmiri carpet. His wife, Marie Louise “Liza” Araneta-Marcos, received a Pashmina shawl in a papier-mâché box. Donald Trump took home a golden Pichwai painting from Nathdwara, Rajasthan, while Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese is the proud new owner of a piece of Jaipur blue pottery.

And the gift-giving went on. Modi gave a Katan silk stole in a Sadheli box to Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi. He bestowed a rose quartz elephant with gold work upon Lao PM Sonexay Siphandone. To Singapore’s PM he conveyed a traditional gond painting. He delivered a Chola bronze sculpture to Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto.

The Nathdwara school of miniature painting, of which Trump was given a representative gift, flourished during the 18th and 19th centuries in the village of the same name in southern Rajasthan, as the Times of India wrote in 2008, on the occasion of an exhibition organized by the Archer Foundation at Amdavad-ni-Gufa, a gallery in Ahmedabad, India. A group of priests had moved a treasured idol of Shrinathji to a new temple there in 1672, explains the Times , after Mughal…
items.t: Trump Accepts Artistic Gift from India Just Months After Branding it a “Hellhole” Country

items.title: New York City’s Transit System Has the State’s Greatest ‘Underground Museum.’ Here’s Why It’s Worth Visiting.
items.summary:
New York has the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum, the Frick Collection, and countless other great art institutions. Yet one of the city’s most well-rounded ones is an “underground museum” that can be found largely in the subway, with certain pieces also visible at Metro-North and Long Island Rail Road train stops.

That was the terminology used by Tina Vaz, director of the MTA’s Arts & Design program, in a talk held this past Friday at the PMC Studio as part of Art Week NYC , a festival of programming put on across the city by ARTnews , Artforum , and Art in America .

“This is a dynamic transit environment, but even in all of the noise and movement and motion, the works get through and people connect with them,” Vaz said. She cited a survey in which 80 percent of respondents said they noticed the artworks at MTA, Metro-North, and LIRR stops, which have been done by artists ranging from William Wegman to Yayoi Kusama. That people were aware of these works, Vaz said, is “double proof of concept.”

Vaz’s latest commissions are by artists Ivan Forde, Trevor Paglen, and Howardena Pindell, who are respectively in the process of making new works for the Broadway Junction subway stop and the Metro-North’s Southeast and Botanical Garden stops. Forde and Pindell joined Vaz on Friday to discuss their commissions.

Forde’s, a mosaic called Bedtime Story for Brownsville: The Fish Who Carried the Moon (2026), grew out of his sketches and poetry. In his mosaic, the Moon is what he called a “main character.” “The Moon has lost her way, and she…
items.t: New York City’s Transit System Has the State’s Greatest ‘Underground Museum.’ Here’s Why It’s Worth Visiting.

Frieze Abu Dhabi makes its debut this week amid geopolitical uncertainty in the region, as the US and Israel’s war in Iran continues to cause concerns about traveling to the Gulf. Even still, the United Arab Emirates is expecting smooth sailing. “It’s business as usual in Abu Dhabi,” Dyala Nusseibeh, Frieze Abu Dhabi’s director, told ARTnews . “The collectors are spending and people are buying.”

Not everyone is so confident that Frieze Abu Dhabi will be a success, however. Beyond the ongoing conflicts, the fair also clashes with the marquee New York evening sales, where high-value, single-owner collections of Theodore and Ruth Baum, Herbert Lust, and the Blaquier-Arrieta family are being offered. “Frieze is a diabolical date—all of us can’t go because we’re all in New York,” Philip Hoffman, chairman and founder of the Fine Art Group, told ARTnews , noting that he thinks people are less likely to go to the fair when the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opens next month. “We’re all wondering what on earth Frieze [is doing] because they can’t get any VIPs ahead of the big sales. New York is where it’s all happening, why on earth would we all go to Frieze?”

items.title: How “American Gothic” Took On a Life of Its Own
items.summary:
You already know the image by heart: Two stern figures stand before an old wooden house. To the left, a blonde, blue-eyed woman wears an apron and a somber expression. Beside her, an unsmiling man in glasses and overalls grips a pitchfork. Since it was first exhibited at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1930, Grant Wood’s painting has joined the ranks of art historical touchstones and shown up in countless ads, books, and memes. But what made this unassuming image so popular, and why does it continue to captivate us today?

In The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon (2026), art historian and curator Wanda M. Corn provides some compelling answers. The author began writing about Wood’s painting in 1981, and she has spent decades amassing an archive of “American Gothic”-related imagery that tracks the farm couple across General Mills cereal ads , Gordon Parks’s 1942 portrait of African-American janitor Ella Watson during his fellowship with the Farm Security Administration, magazine covers, COVID-era cartoons, and other surprising riffs. Her book traces the painting’s history from the controversy behind its creation and the bitter fallout it brought to its hapless maker through to its transformation into a pop culture cornerstone and a symbol of Wood’s home state.

Grant Wood, "Self-portrait" (1932), oil on masonite (image public domain CC0 via the Friends of Art Acquisition Fund )
items.t: How “American Gothic” Took On a Life of Its Own

items.title: Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy
items.summary:
Almeida theatre, London
Part-Phaedra and part-Medea, Gough is mesmerising in Ebenezer Bamgboye’s stylised staging of Eugene O’Neill’s family drama

You would not know that Eugene O’Neill’s play was originally set on a mid 19th-century farm. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land.

It makes for a strange mix at first, beguiling and bewildering in equal measure. Bamgboye employs some of the striking theatricality that he brought to his magnetic adaptation of The Lonely Londoners two years ago. It is an original refashioning, the script sharper with less of the exposition that might date it, but the directorial flourishes come so thick and fast that it is stylised to the bone. Bamgboye has previously worked with Rebecca Frecknall (who staged the leaden O’Neill drama A Moon for the Misbegotten last year) and the first half seems to pay too big a debt to her style of work.

items.title: Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works
items.summary:
Conceptual artist Eleanor Antin is seeking the return of at least 179 works or $975,000 in compensatory damages in a lawsuit against her dealer, Richard Saltoun. The complaint was filed in New York State Supreme Court on July 29, six months after the artist terminated her relationship with Saltoun’s namesake gallery, which operates locations in New York, London, and Rome.

Filed by the 91-year-old artist’s son and attorney-in-fact, Blaise Antin, and her studio, Paranoid Productions, the suit claims that Saltoun “initially purported to agree to return all of the works it held” upon their business separation at the gallery's London location on January 16. News of the lawsuit was first reported by Artnet . 

Saltoun claimed in February that the gallery had returned all of Antin’s works to her family, according to filed documents. However, later that month, the artist’s archivist, citing an inventory produced by Saltoun himself, allegedly discovered that Antin was still missing at least 179 works, the majority of which were still held at the London gallery.
items.t: Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works

items.title: Anti-Monuments to Trump
items.summary:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, I was in the last place I wanted to be: Washington, DC. Where would I go? I wanted nothing to do with his administration’s empty grandeur. I spent the day at Maya Lin’s Vietnam War Memorial, a dark wound in the earth. In this much more hopeful moment post-midterms, Ed Simon asks a related question: How should memorials remember the MAGA era? He points to historical anti-fascist examples in Germany — and also suggests the bulldozing of Trump’s ballroom to rubble as its own kind of monument. 

Satire’s not a bad strategy to record this era, either. Also today, Greg Werkheiser pens an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act. The act’s next of kin, the National Register of Historic Places, he writes, “is said to be concerned about its own health.”

Finally, don’t miss the newest installation of Jennifer Samet’s “Beer With a Painter” column. She interviews Ivorian painter Ouattara Watts, who works only at night, when the veil between this world and the next is thinnest. Plus, The Met and the Shanghai Museum are teaming up, just weeks after MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Museum joined forces. They say art imitates life; I just didn’t know that meant we were getting museum oligopolies.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor 

How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy. | Ed Simon

items.title: Valerie Solanas’s obscenely funny Scum Manifesto is an unignorable burst of female outrage | Emily Woof
items.summary:
Before an assassination attempt on Andy Warhol in 1968, Solanas used her fierce writing to confront male supremacy. What can her work teach us about expressing raw anger?

It is exhausting to always express anger constructively and reasonably – especially when what you are angry about is violence, exploitation and the inexcusable appetite of disgusting, powerful, greedy men to gain yet more power.

Could you please be more balanced in how you express yourself? Could you make your objection to the destruction of the world – through violating not only women but also the planet – well, more constructive? Could you be a little less unpleasant in your anger?

items.title: Rare Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction
items.summary:
Hilma af Klint, “Ser III No. 5” (1920) (image via Bukowskis ) Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic's writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us . 

Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction Works by the Swedish spiritualist and abstract art pioneer, who asked that her paintings remain unseen for 20 years after her death in 1944, have not come up for auction in more than three decades. That's about to change with the emergence of “ Ser III No. 5 ” (1920) at the Stockholm-based house Bukowskis , which estimates the oil and graphite on canvas will fetch up to 8 million SEK (~$791,000) in its upcoming November 18–19 sale. Controversy has long followed the legacy of the late artist , with some arguing that her works should be kept together rather than sold and commercialized .

Sotheby's Settles Dispute With Heirs Who Contested Van Gogh Sale After the heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer requested the withdrawal of Van Gogh's “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (1890) from a sale at Sotheby's, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe, the family has reached a “mutually satisfactory resolution” with the work's consignors, said a Sotheby's statement shared with Hyperallergic. But will the dispute put a damper on sale results? We'll find out tomorrow night when the painting, valued at $180 million, goes under the hammer.
items.t: Rare Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction

items.title: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?
items.summary:
At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for. 

When the “ Monument Against Fascism ” was unveiled in 1986, it was a 40-foot-tall (~12.2 m) rectangular aluminum pillar covered in lead sheeting on which Hamburg residents were invited to inscribe their own pledges to fight authoritarianism. Over the next seven years, the column was lowered into the ground in stages, so that today the monument is entirely subterranean, visible only through a small glass window next to the plaque. 

Designed by married conceptual artists Esther Shalev-Gerz and Jochen Gerz and commissioned by the Municipal Council of Hamburg-Harburg, the monument was intended to confront both Germany’s Nazi past and the reemergence of far-right politics in a provocative, arresting manner that purposefully eschewed the monumental architecture that fascists themselves exalted. The result was Shalev-Gerz and Gerz’s consummate anti-monument, a reminder that the war against fascism is as personal as someone’s handwriting and as continual as the ground beneath our feet.
items.t: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

items.title: Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work
items.summary:
A new joint video exhibition has opened above 14th Street on the High Line, featuring three moving-image works that illustratively dissect and defy the economic legacies of the British Empire's grip on South Asia and China. Screening daily until January 11, Between Salt and Smoke presents two animated videos by Pakistani-American artist Shahzia Sikander and one documented performance by artists Himali Singh Soin and David Soin Tappeser, who make up the duo Hylozoic/Desires. 

The artists examine British colonial extraction and violence in Asia through the lens of the East India Company's monopolies on salt, opium, and other highly valued goods. A new work by Sikander, “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026), consists of hand-painted images that the artist digitally animated in a research-driven cinematic exploration of trade history between the declining Mughal Empire, the East India Company, and the Qing Dynasty. 

Shahzia Sikander, still from “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026) (image courtesy the artist)
items.t: Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work

items.title: ‘How can we make it riskier?’: the trans theatre troupe turning Virginia Woolf’s Orlando into a ‘porno-biography’
items.summary:
A radical new take on the modernist classic includes a Berlin ketamine binge, a ‘goon cave’ and an all-trans cast. The manifesto? To ‘desecrate’ expectations

As Orlando’s on a comedown after a ket-heavy night out in Berlin, surrounded by a group of sharp-tongued trans sex workers, Charli Cowgill and Laurie Ward pause the read-through. The scene is new and “it’s feeling a little safe,” Ward says, drumming the table. “How can we make it riskier?”

Cowgill and Ward are piss/CARNATION, a theatre-making duo creating fearless, messy and intellectually rigorous work. Audience spit was collected and thrown in their first production, 52 Monologues for Young Transsexuals, a show that collated trans women’s experiences of men and sex work. Ugly Sisters, the pair’s riotous follow-up, relived a brief encounter between a trans woman and Germaine Greer who wrote a caustic article about it. “As a company,” Ward says, “we tend more towards brutal than twee.”

items.title: The play that changed my life: ‘John Berger’s Pig Earth became something magical – they licked milk off bodies’
items.summary:
The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol by Complicité conjured the struggles of a French village with an intense rawness

There are many things you see that are impactful, but few you can genuinely say change your life. I saw Complicité’s The Three Lives of Lucie Cabrol aged 16 on a school trip to Riverside Studios in London and it really reached me. I’d been educated in a very language, words-based way. Here the story was told – with such intensity! – through people’s bodies.

The world they were conjuring, from a story by John Berger in his book Pig Earth, was about this remote French village – a world of labour. And the strife and struggles of these characters was expressed through the physical work of the company.

items.title: Souped-up and now on screen, Starlight Express is moving in all sorts of ways
items.summary:
Luke Sheppard’s revival of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s 80s musical is in cinemas and going on tour. What gives these ridiculous, rollerskating trains such emotional force?

I hardly ever cry at the theatre but can think of three recent cases. 1. The beautifully jittery balcony scene in Liverpool Everyman’s Romeo and Juliet. 2. Dear Theodosia as co-sung by Leslie Odom Jr (actual OG Aaron Burr!) in Hamilton. 3. An embarrassingly large amount of Starlight Express.

Why on earth does this ridiculous fantasy of rollerskating trains, with their high-speed scrapes, leave me feeling like an emotional wreck? That’s what happened when I first saw director Luke Sheppard’s souped-up London revival – and again this month, watching a new film of that production.

items.summary:
Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing

Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.

“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”

items.title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
items.summary:
Orange Tree theatre, London
This streamlined adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel gets right to the heart of her characters, who face heartbreak and loss but gain from the strength of female friendship

There’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon. Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the lovable humour and sentiment as it did so.

This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna and Josh Roche, bypasses all those dangers by leaning into theatricality – and sheer good acting. The script is by Coghlan and McKenna, who previously adapted The Forsyte Saga, staged last year by the RSC. They confidently fillet the original and also add their own little inventions.

Continue reading...
items.t: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
